items.abstract: Background/Objectives: This study evaluates the adaptation of a novel filling material (Odne®Fill, Switzerland) to the walls of the shaped root canal using micro-computed tomography. Methods: Fourteen extracted human molars (6 maxillary and 8 mandibular), comprising a total of 32 root canals, were included. After canal preparation, all canals were filled with Odne®Fill according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Periapical radiographs and micro-computed tomography were used to assess the extent of canal wall coverage by the filling material. Surface coverage was quantified by image segmentation and statistically analyzed. Results: The percentage of canal wall coverage ranged from 93.31% to 99.98%. The mean coverage rate was 97.63% (SD 1.70%) and the median was 98.23%, indicating a high degree of adaptation of the filling material to the ex vivo prepared canal walls. Conclusions: Under the conditions of this ex vivo study Odne®Fill demonstrated high canal wall adaptation values. These findings should be interpreted with caution and further com-parative and long-term studies are required before clinical relevance can be established.

items.abstract: Mandibular reconstruction restores facial continuity and oral function after segmental resection. Patient-specific cutting guides transfer a computed tomography (CT)-based plan to the operating room with three-dimensional information, but printed guides add cost and lead time, cannot adapt after fabrication, and may interrupt surgery if sterility is lost. We investigate a markerless augmented reality (AR) alternative that registers a virtual cutting guide to the exposed mandible from surface geometry. The method extends surface-based registration for the transoral setting, where teeth form the most distinctive visible surface. After camera calibration, a HoloLens 2 time-of-flight camera captures a partial intraoperative point cloud. The user supplies a rough head-based alignment only to crop the region of interest. A teeth-weighted global stage computes correspondences and solves a truncated least-squares rigid alignment. An asymmetric point-to-plane iterative closest point (ICP) stage refines the complete CT mandible against the partial depth cloud target. The guide-to-mandible transform places the guide in the HoloLens world frame, while pose updates and interpolation follow target motion. We define a blinded phantom protocol with 30 target registration error (TRE) points under full, intermediate, and teeth-only exposure, plus a motion-to-display latency test. Our median TRE is 4.05, 6.10, and 7.10 mm respectively, and median latency is 0.805 s. These values support the feasibility of using AR to replace physical prints. The workflow removes mounted fiducials and manual landmark selection and provides a testable path toward transoral cutting guidance.

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The three‐dimensional (3D) facial soft tissue response to premolar extraction remains unclear, particularly in relation to vertical skeletal changes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Thirty‐three adult women who underwent orthodontic treatment with the extraction of four premolars were included. Homologous facial models were generated from facial soft‐tissue surface data derived from CBCT images acquired before and after treatment. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed to characterise variation in facial form using homologous model coordinates. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was used to evaluate components nominally associated with pre‐ and post‐treatment configurations within each vertical skeletal subgroup.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Each vertical skeletal subgroup included 11 subjects. In the decreased‐FMA group, PC5 showed the largest nominal AUC (0.79), followed by PC3 and PC11 (both 0.75), with morphological variation concentrated in the lower facial region. In the increased‐FMA group, PC7 and PC12 showed nominal AUCs of 0.76 and 0.73, respectively, and were associated with lateral facial narrowing and facial slimming. No meaningful nominal discrimination was identified in the stable‐FMA group. These findings indicated distinct group‐level morphological tendencies depending on the direction of vertical skeletal change.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three‐dimensional facial soft‐tissue changes following premolar extraction showed group‐level patterns that appeared to vary according to the direction of vertical skeletal change. Patients with decreased FMA tended to show lower facialreorganisation, whereas patients with increased FMA tended to show lateral facial narrowing and facial slimming. Given the modest subgroup size and multiple nominal ROC comparisons, these findings warrant confirmation in larger cohorts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The article presents first insights to radiocarbon dating of taxonomically diverse Pleistocene faunal assemblage recovered from Graniczna Cave in the Kraków-Częstochowa Upland. The material represents one of the most heterogeneous cave bone accumulations in the region, comprising remains of large and small mammals. Thirteen bone samples representing different taxa were selected for AMS radiocarbon dating, and one sediment sample was analyzed using optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) to provide an independent chronological reference. The study primarily focuses on the variable preservation state of bone collagen, which plays a critical role in the reliability of radiocarbon dating. This study highlights the inherent difficulties of dating cave-derived bone assemblages and emphasizes the need for rigorous pre-screening criteria, including collagen quality assessment and elemental composition.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:list>
                      <jats:list-item>
                        <jats:p>Geometric morphometrics (GM) is widely used to study phenotypic variation in ecological and evolutionary research, but the throughput of manual landmark digitization limits how large morphometric datasets can practically become, especially in field studies that would benefit from rapid on‐site feedback.</jats:p>
                      </jats:list-item>
                      <jats:list-item>
                        <jats:p>
                          We introduce
                          <jats:italic>Theia</jats:italic>
                          , an edge‐AI mobile framework that performs end‐to‐end GM workflows directly on‐device, including image acquisition, automated landmark detection and morphometric analysis. The system integrates a dual‐stage deep‐learning pipeline with an offline analytical engine implementing generalized procrustes analysis (GPA) and principal component analysis (PCA), enabling field‐based analyses on low‐cost mobile hardware.
                        </jats:p>
                      </jats:list-item>
                      <jats:list-item>
                        <jats:p>
                          Validation against the geomorph R package demonstrated near‐perfect computational fidelity (|
                          <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                          | > 0.999). Comparisons with expert manual digitization across 268 held‐out specimens showed close morphospace concordance, with biological variation accounting for 92.9% of total shape variance and the method effect (AI vs. manual) for 0.5%. The method effect is small, so the shape ordination used in downstream analysis is preserved.
                        </jats:p>
                      </jats:list-item>
                      <jats:list-item>
                        <jats:p>
                          <jats:italic>Theia</jats:italic>
                          enables standardized, reproducible morphometric data collection directly in the field. It complements established desktop workflows and suits studies that need portability and on‐site quality control, such as large‐scale spatial sampling and long‐term monitoring.
                        </jats:p>
                      </jats:list-item>
                    </jats:list>
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Recent studies have shown that murine and avian Meissner‐like corpuscles are innervated by two distinct mechanoreceptor afferents with different functional properties. In addition, there is evidence that one subpopulation of Meissner corpuscles of monkeys is doubly innervated by mechanoreceptors and nociceptors. In humans, however, most Meissner corpuscles are supplied by a single axon. In the present study, different techniques were used (silver impregnation, immunohistochemistry for axon markers, axonal 3D reconstruction, and double immunofluorescence associated with confocal laser microscopy) to analyze whether human digital Meissner's corpuscles have double innervation. The percentage of Meissner corpuscles with apparent double innervation was minimal, about 2%, but these data were not confirmed when sections processed for double immunofluorescence for peripherin plus neurofilament proteins or TrkB plus Ret were analyzed. In fact, TrkB co‐localized with Ret in the axon of Meissner's corpuscles. In the 3D axonal reconstructions, there was no evidence of double innervation but the single axon had different calibers along its path and very fine collateral protrusions. The present results demonstrate that most human digital Meissner's corpuscles (around 95–98%) are innervated by a single axon in which TrkB and Ret co‐localize, instead of being supplied by two independent TrkB‐ and Ret‐positive axons as occurs in other species.</jats:p>
authors: Patricia Cuendias, Yolanda García‐Mesa, Iván Suazo, Marta Alonso‐Guervós, Jorge García‐Piqueras, Ana M. Abreu‐Velez, Olivia García‐Suárez, Jorge Feito, José A. Vega

items.title: Human digital Meissner's corpuscles are not doubly innervated
